analysis.one_liner: Lets the FDA temporarily import foreign versions of scarce prescription drugs and fast-track generic competition in markets with few rivals.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2025 with a bipartisan group of four senators and referred to the Senate Health Committee, where it has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: When a prescription drug is in shortage, the FDA would have to authorize temporary imports of the same active ingredient from countries where it is already legally sold, as long as the maker plans to seek U.S. generic approval. It also creates a new category, 'marginally competitive drug markets' — older off-patent drugs where fewer than five approved versions are actually sold — and treats those markets like shortages, triggering the same import authority plus expedited review of new generic applications. The import authority ends after three years or once the shortage ends.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who depend on drugs that are hard to fill — chemotherapy agents, anesthetics, antibiotics, and other hospital staples that have repeatedly gone into shortage. If the bill becomes law, pharmacists and hospitals would have a backup supply, and prices on old drugs with only a handful of sellers would face new competition.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to authorize temporary importation of a drug facing a shortage if it is lifesaving, life-sustaining, or treats a debilitating condition, is already lawfully marketed in certain foreign countries, and has the same active ingredient as the drug in shortage — with importation beginning within 60 days of a qualifying application.

Treats 'marginally competitive' markets — drugs approved at least 10 years ago, off-patent, with fewer than five commercially available approved versions — as shortages for importation purposes and lets the FDA expedite generic applications and inspections for those drugs.

Counts an application holder's multiple approved versions of the same drug as only one competitor and counts drugs that have been discontinued or withdrawn as not commercially available, closing a common way of padding the appearance of competition.
The import authority is temporary — it ends after three years or when the shortage is resolved, whichever comes first — and the FDA can deny importation on safety or effectiveness grounds.

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers — brand-name or generic — whose old off-patent drugs currently face little competition. They would lose the ability to keep prices high on drugs with a captive market, and foreign versions would temporarily take sales during shortages. Taxpayers also bear the FDA's added review and importation-oversight workload.

drawbacks.text: Imported drugs would come from foreign supply chains, and while the FDA can deny imports on safety or effectiveness grounds, some imports would enter before full U.S. approval, which carries some quality-assurance risk.

Temporary importation treats the symptom, not the cause: many shortages stem from domestic manufacturing quality failures and thin profit margins on old generics, which this bill does not fix and which could even further squeeze the economics of making low-margin generics in the U.S.

Drawing supply from foreign markets during a shortage could shift scarcity to the exporting countries unless supply is sufficient, a trade-off the bill addresses only through the FDA's discretionary denial authority.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing a life-threatening drug shortage, a safe backup supply within 60 days is a real and immediate benefit, and the temporary, shortage-triggered design limits the risk of permanently bypassing U.S. approval. The main honest objection is that the bill manages shortages rather than preventing them: it does not address why so many old, essential drugs are made by only a few firms at fragile margins. It is a targeted, reasonable stopgap, not a full fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and read twice in the Senate, then referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on July 17, 2025, and no hearing, markup, or vote has happened since.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on July 17, 2025, joined by original cosponsors Sens. Mike Lee, Dick Durbin, and Chuck Grassley — a mix of two Democrats and two Republicans.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and PENSIONS the same day; the action history shows no further steps.
The Congress is still in session, so the bill could still move, but it has not yet received any committee consideration.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, the small group of manufacturers that controls supply of old off-patent drugs keeps its captive markets, and patients continue to face shortages while the bill waits in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support is evenly split by party — one Democrat and two Republicans joined the Democratic sponsor at introduction — and no opposition has appeared on the record, so the fight so far is about inaction rather than party lines.

industries.industry: Manufacturers of old off-patent drugs with few competitors
industries.note: These firms hold approved applications for essential older drugs that few others make, which lets them keep prices high when competitors exit. The bill opens their markets to temporary imports and expedited generics whenever fewer than five versions are actually sold, costing them sales and price power during shortages and in long-running thin-competition markets.

Firms already lawfully selling shortage drugs in listed foreign countries would gain a temporary U.S. sales channel, and they must commit to seeking U.S. generic approval as a condition. Their entry is what gives patients the backup supply.

Health providers spend significant time and money managing shortages — rationing doses and hunting for supply — and a mandated import pathway within 60 days would ease that burden and reduce patient harm from delayed or missed treatments.

analysis.trajectory: Most Senate bills never get a committee hearing, and this one has seen no action since referral. Its best realistic path is being folded into a broader FDA or drug-shortage package, where Sen. Grassley's involvement helps; a standalone floor vote is unlikely without committee movement.
